verdict: OK to lend in Kolhapur sugar & ethanol, but only to integrated mills with distillery cushion and clean cane-payment record; avoid pure-standalone mills and any account with arrears building.
title: Kolhapur Sugar & Ethanol: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A Kolhapur mill crushes cane for roughly a five-month season, converts juice into sugar and molasses, and now increasingly diverts juice/B-heavy molasses into ethanol. Cash arrives in two streams: sugar sold through the year and ethanol supplied to OMCs. **The mill's real product is timing — it buys cane in a short window and sells sugar over twelve months, so the balance sheet is a working-capital machine, not a factory.** Kolhapur sugar is quoted at ₹3,845/qtl and C-heavy ethanol at ₹56.8/L [1]; FRP is ₹340/qtl [1]. Cane cost is the single largest line and is politically set, so pricing power sits with the government, not the mill. Capex is lumpy and distillery-led — one peer spent ~₹70 crore on refining capacity funded by internal accruals, lifting realisations by ~₹0.5–1.0/kg [9].

## What has changed now
**The local cane price is unsettled: millers and farmers remain divided in Kolhapur, and a joint meeting is promised but not held [2][3].** That is the live risk — an unresolved cane price means arrears can build before the season's cash comes in. Rating commentary flags exactly this: government support via remunerative ethanol prices and interest subvention is what prevents cane arrears piling up, and integrated mills are better placed than standalone ones [10]. Peer results are healthier than the local news: Triveni's Q1 FY27 saw improved profitability and reduced debt on strong sugar and distillery margins [5], and EID Parry's realisation rose to ₹51.2/kg from ₹43.7/kg on premium mix [6]. Note the Simbhaoli UP mill sale [1] is a UP distress story, not Kolhapur — read it as a warning on leveraged standalone mills, not as local news. Sources say little specific about Kolhapur mill balance sheets; lean on first principles and peers.

## Where to grow
**Pursue integrated mills with a running distillery and a clean cane-payment record, and the cane growers'/co-operative structures that feed them.** The ethanol leg is the growth engine: remunerative ethanol prices plus interest subvention for debt-funded distillery capex are the stated supports [10]. Also look at premium/consumer-pack sugar players — the realisation gap between bulk and premium is real [6]. Avoid standalone mills with no distillery, mills with visible cane arrears, and any group showing the Simbhaoli pattern of debt-driven mill sales [1].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the season, not the year: cash-flow-backed limits sized to one crush, with cane-payment escrow and monthly stock-and-arrer statements.** Take every month: cane arrears outstanding, sugar stock and free stock, ethanol supply invoices/OMC receivables, and distillery utilisation. Covenant on gearing and interest cover — peer rating work shows gearing ~1.4x and interest cover around 2x as the moderated norm [11]. When a proposal lands, check the cane price assumption against the unresolved Kolhapur deadlock [2]; if the mill is assuming a settled price, ask for the sensitivity at the FRP of ₹340/qtl [1].

## Early-warning signs
- Cane arrears rising month-on-month (monthly) → freeze fresh limits and ask for the payment plan.
- Sugar realisations drifting below ₹3,845/qtl [1] (monthly) → re-run stock valuation and margin.
- Ethanol offtake or OMC receivable ageing stretching (monthly) → tighten drawing power.
- Any sign of mill divestment or group restructuring (quarterly) → treat as the Simbhaoli signal [1] and review exposure.
watch: Arrears rise two months running -> freeze fresh limits, demand escrow funding
Falls below quoted level -> revalue stock, cut drawing power
Ageing stretches beyond agreed days -> tighten limit, seek assignment
Falls sharply -> ask for cause, review ethanol-linked cash flow
Any mill sale signal [1] -> immediate exposure review
